title: Kasparov against Topalov, 1999: a king hunt across the whole board
outcomes: Tries each of the five key moments before seeing the move and compares the attempt with the engine's first choice
Says what the engine's rating does and does not show about the sacrifice at move 24: level at depth 16, not a proven win
Tells which of White's moves in the hunt were checks or captures and which were quiet

steps.text: **Kasparov (White) against Topalov (Black)**, round 4 of the Hoogovens tournament, Wijk aan Zee, January 1999. A Pirc Defense in which both sides castled queenside; by move 23 Black's king stood on a7. You will play White at five moments and compare your move with the engine's first choice and with the game. Engine ratings are evidence at a stated depth, not proof; close moves can change order with depth.

steps.caption: Moves 19 to 23. Step through them; the first decision comes at the end.

line.say: Qf4 gives check on the diagonal to b8.
The king steps to a7.
Black's pawn advances to d4.
The knight goes to d5, where Black can take it.
Black takes with the knight from b6.
White's e-pawn recaptures.
The queen goes to d6. White to move: your first decision is next.

claims.statement: White's king is on the queenside.
Black's king is on the queenside.

steps.caption: After 24.Rxd4 it is Black's turn: take the rook or decline it. Engine numbers are from White's side.

line.say: Black took the rook with the pawn. At depth 16 the engine prefers the quiet 24...Kb6, which declines.

claims.statement: 24...cxd4 is legal.
At depth 16 the engine's top move for Black is Kb6.
At depth 16 the engine does not rate this position as better for White: level, or better for Black by at most 1.2 pawns.

steps.caption: After 25.Re7+. Black does not have to take the rook. The game went on like this.

line.say: Topalov did not take the rook. His king stepped to b6.
Qxd4+ takes the pawn on d4 with check.
The king takes the knight on a5.

claims.statement: 25...Qxe7 was legal.
25...Kb6 is legal.

steps.caption: Not played: what if Black had taken the rook with the queen (25...Qxe7)? White to move.

line.say: Qxd4+ begins a forced mate. The engine at depth 16 finds mate in four from here.
The king goes to b8.
Qb6+ is check.
The bishop blocks on b7.
Nc6+ is check again.
The king goes to a8.
Qa7 is checkmate.

claims.statement: White mates in four moves starting with Qxd4+.

steps.caption: Moves 27 to 35, the hunt across the board. Watch which moves are checks and which are not.

line.say: b4 is check. The pawn is defended (by the pawn on a3 and by the queen), so the king cannot take it.
The king goes to a4.
Qc3 is neither a check nor a capture.
Black's queen takes the pawn on d5.
Ra7 attacked the bishop on a8. It went to b7 and the rook took it.
The queen takes the knight on f6.
Black's king takes the pawn on a3.
Qxa6+ takes a pawn with check.
c3 is a pawn check. The king takes the pawn.
Black's king has walked from a7 to d1.

claims.statement: 27.b4+ is legal.
After b4 two white pieces defend the pawn.

steps.prompt: Look back at White's nine moves from 27 to 35.

fields.label: How many were neither a check nor a capture?

steps.caption: 36.Bf1. Engine numbers depend on depth: a single-line search rates this position level at depth 16 and clearly better for White at depth 22. Evidence, not proof.

line.say: Bf1 attacks the queen on c4. The pawn on b5 defends it.
Black's rook goes to d2, next to its king.

claims.statement: After Bf1 one white piece attacks the queen on c4.
After Bf1 one black piece defends the queen on c4.
In a single-line search at depth 16 the engine rates this position roughly level (within 0.8 of a pawn).
In a single-line search at depth 22 the engine rates this position at least one pawn better for White.

steps.caption: Not played: 37.Bxc4 takes the queen. At depth 16 the engine rates the position after it as level. Black to move.

line.say: The black rook takes the white queen on b2.
The king takes the rook.
The pawn takes the bishop. Each side has a rook.

claims.statement: In a four-line search at depth 16 the engine's first choice for Black is Rxb2.
At depth 16 the engine rates the position after 37.Bxc4 roughly level (within 0.8 of a pawn).

steps.caption: 37.Rd7 and the end of the game. Settings matter here: a four-line search at depth 16 puts Rd7 first, a single-line search at depth 16 rates the position level, and a single-line search at depth 22 rates it at least two pawns better for White. Evidence, not proof. Black resigned after 44.Qa7 (Wikipedia).

line.say: Rd7: the rook goes to d7, where the black rook can take it.
Black's rook takes it.
Now the bishop takes the queen.
The b5 pawn takes the bishop.
The queen takes the rook on h8. White now has a queen and three pawns against a rook and four pawns.
Qa7. Black resigned here: 1-0.

claims.statement: 37.Rd7 is legal.
In a single-line search at depth 16 the engine rates the position before 37.Rd7 roughly level (within 0.8 of a pawn).
In a single-line search at depth 22 the engine rates the position before 37.Rd7 at least two pawns better for White.
In a four-line search at depth 16 the engine's first choice is Rd7.

steps.prompt: After 24.Rxd4 the engine, at depth 16, did not rate the position better for White. In one sentence: what does that show about the sacrifice, and what does it not show?

steps.text: **What the game shows.** After the sacrifice at move 24 the engine, at depth 16, does not rate White better; at depth 22 it rates White at least a pawn better before 36.Bf1. Core skills: types of sacrifice, attacking the castled king, checks-captures-threats, forced-mate search. Of White's 16 moves from 24 to 39, 12 gave check or captured; 28.Qc3, 29.Ra7, 36.Bf1 and 37.Rd7 did neither.

steps.prompt: Which of the five moments (24.Rxd4, 25.Re7+, 27.b4+, 36.Bf1, 37.Rd7) would you have missed in a game of your own, and what would you have had to notice to find it?
